Modal music. Modal music is a system of melody and improvisation organized around modes—recurring melodic and harmonic frameworks distinct from Western major and minor tonality. Prevalent in Indian classical music through ragas, Persian and Arabic music through dastgah and maqam, and many non-Western traditions, modal systems offer a fundamentally different approach to pitch organization. Rather than functional harmony progressing toward tonal centers, modal music explores the subtle emotional and coloristic possibilities of a single pitch framework. In Western medieval and Renaissance music, modes like Ionian, Dorian, and Phrygian preceded the major-minor tonality system. Non-Western modal systems are independent of Western tonality and reflect different aesthetic priorities: color, ornamentation, and spiritual resonance over harmonic progression. Ragas in Hindustani classical music are intricate melodic frameworks with prescribed ascending and descending patterns, emotional associations, and time-of-day usage. Dastgah in Persian music and maqam in Arabic music similarly organize melody around a tonal center, embellished with microtonal inflections like quarter-tones unavailable in Western tuning. Modal improvisation often involves exploring a single pitch framework deeply rather than modulating through multiple keys as in Western jazz or classical forms. Western jazz musicians, especially after the nineteen fifties, adopted modal thinking from Indian and African music, creating a synthesis exemplified by Miles Davis' Kind of Blue. The distinction between modal and tonal music is philosophical as much as technical: modal systems prioritize color and emotion within a framework, while tonal systems prioritize functional harmony.
